english_translation: Come here and help me lift these heavy things.

dialogue.shona: Uyai kuno mundibatsire kusimudza zvinhu zvinorema izvi.
dialogue.english: Come here and help me lift these heavy things.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Uyai [come! (polite/plural)] • kuno [here / to this place] • mundibatsire [in / singular ndibatsire] • kusimudza [to / at simudza] • zvinhu [things nhu] • zvinorema [things norema] • izvi [izvi]

grammar_notes.title: Giving Commands & Polite Requests ('Uyai')
grammar_notes.content: Notice the command verb 'Uyai' in this sentence. In Shona, a direct command to one person (singular) is simply the verb stem ending in '-a'—for example, 'Vhara!' ('Close!'), 'Tora!' ('Take!'), or 'Huya!' ('Come!'). When speaking to more than one person, or when showing polite respect to an adult, you add '-i' to the end, changing '-a' to '-ai' (as in 'Huyai!' = 'Come!' or 'Batai!' = 'Catch/Hold!'). Adding the prefix 'chi-' (as in 'Chiuya' or 'Chigara') means 'Do it right now'.
grammar_notes.rule: Singular Command: Verb stem (-a) [Huya! / Tora!] | Polite or Plural Command: Verb stem + -i (-ai) [Huyai! / Torai!]

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('zvinorema')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvinorema' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Pointing Out Things: Demonstratives ('kuno' = 'this / that / here')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, words for 'this/these' and 'that/those' (like 'kuno') come AFTER the noun they point to and mirror the noun's group! Near demonstratives ('this / these / right here') repeat the noun class vowel: 'mwana uyu' (this child), 'nyama iyi' (this meat), 'kapu iyi' (this cup), 'bhuku iri' (this book), 'zvinhu izvi' (these things). Replacing the final vowel with '-o' shifts the meaning to 'that / those / there': 'uyo' (that person), 'iyo' (that one), 'uko' (over there).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Near Demonstrative ('uyu/iyi/iri/ichi/izvi' = this/these) | replace final vowel with '-o' ('uyo/iyo/iro/icho/izvo' = that/those)

cultural_notes.title: Lending a Hand ('Kubatsirana') with Heavy Loads
cultural_notes.content: In Zimbabwean neighbourhoods and rural homesteads alike, nobody is left to carry heavy loads ('zvinhu zvinorema') alone. Calling out 'Uyai kuno mundibatsire!' ('Come here and help me!') invites younger relatives or neighbours to share the weight—embodying the proverb 'Rume rimwe harikombi churu' ('One person alone cannot surround an anthill').

active_exercises.prompt: How would you say 'Open the door quickly!' in Shona using the vocabulary pattern from this unit?

Put the cup on the table before you leave.
Close the window because it is cold outside.
Come here and help me carry the books.

active_exercises.prompt: If someone says 'Ndinonzwa nyota, ndinoda kunwa mukaka kana mvura', what are they asking for?

Milk or water because they feel thirsty
Maize meal and cooking oil from the market
Salt and vegetables for the evening meal
